questions.question: What does the doctype declaration at the top of an HTML document do?
options: Imports a page template from the server
Switches browsers into standards mode
Loads the page's CSS stylesheet
Declares the human language of the page
questions.rationale: The doctype tells the browser to render in standards mode rather than emulating legacy quirks; the language is declared separately on the html element with lang.

questions.question: Which element should wrap the unique content of the page, appearing exactly once per document?
options: header
nav
main
aside
questions.rationale: main marks the one central content area and maps to the main landmark, letting screen-reader users jump past repeated headers and navigation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a void element — no content and no closing tag?
options: p
div
img
ul
questions.rationale: img is void: it carries only attributes such as src and alt. Elements like p, div, and ul wrap content and must be closed.

questions.question: What is the difference between article and section?
options: They are interchangeable synonyms
article is self-contained content that could stand alone (a post, a product card); section is a themed chapter of the page it lives on
section is used only for images and media
article must always be nested inside nav
questions.rationale: An article makes sense syndicated or on its own page, while a section groups related content within the page and normally starts with its own heading.

questions.question: What is the correct alt attribute for a purely decorative background flourish image?
options: alt="image"
alt="decoration"
No alt attribute at all
alt="" (empty)
questions.rationale: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image entirely; omitting the attribute instead makes them announce the filename, and descriptive alt would be noise.

questions.question: What does a label element connected to a form control through matching for and id values provide?
options: Styling for the input field
A programmatic association: clicking the label focuses the control and screen readers announce it as the field's name
Server-side validation of the field
Automatic submission of the form
questions.rationale: The label-for link is the accessible name of the control; it also enlarges the clickable target, which helps every user.

questions.question: When should a form use method="post" rather than "get"?
options: When the form changes server state or carries sensitive data such as passwords
For search pages so the results are bookmarkable
Never — get is always the correct method
Only when JavaScript is enabled in the browser
questions.rationale: GET puts data in the URL where it is cached and logged, so anything sensitive or state-changing must go in the POST body; GET is right for bookmarkable searches.

questions.question: Why prefer strong over b for important text?
options: Because b is deprecated and no longer renders
Because strong makes text larger
Because they are identical in meaning, only the name differs
Because strong conveys real importance that screen readers announce, while b is purely visual
questions.rationale: Semantic elements carry meaning to assistive technology; b and i are presentational and communicate nothing beyond their look.

questions.question: What is the recommended rule for heading levels (h1 to h6)?
options: Exactly one h1 per page, descending levels without skipping any
As many h1 elements as there are font sizes needed
Use h1 only inside the header element
Choose heading levels by the color and size you want
questions.rationale: Headings form the document outline that screen-reader users navigate by; one h1 with no skipped levels keeps that map intact, while size is CSS's job.

questions.question: What is the 'first rule of ARIA' in accessible web development?
options: Add ARIA roles to every element for safety
ARIA attributes replace the need for alt text
Prefer native semantic elements; reach for ARIA only when no native equivalent exists
ARIA is relevant only to form controls
questions.rationale: A native button already announces itself, is focusable, and handles Enter and Space; ARIA can patch roles onto non-semantic markup but should never be the first choice.
